reminder: A Gaussian integer is a [complex number](c:complex-number) $a+bi$ whose real part $a$ and imaginary part $b$ are [integers](c:integer).
definition: A Gaussian integer is a [complex number](c:complex-number) $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. The Gaussian integers form the [ring](c:ring) $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, with norm $N(a+bi)=a^2+b^2$ and units $\pm1,\pm i$.
examples: The numbers $3+2i$, $-5i$ and $7$ are Gaussian integers.
In $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ the prime $5$ is not prime any more: $5=(2+i)(2-i)$.
Non-example: $\tfrac12+i$ and $1+\sqrt2\,i$ are not Gaussian integers, because one coordinate is not an integer.

steps: Use the norm $N(a+bi)=a^2+b^2$ as the size function on $\mathbb{Z}[i]$.
For $\alpha$ and $\beta\ne0$, round the complex quotient $\alpha/\beta$ to the nearest Gaussian integer $q$.
Each coordinate of the rounding error is at most $1/2$, so $N(\alpha-q\beta)\le N(\beta)/2<N(\beta)$.
So $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ has division with remainder, and it is a [Euclidean domain](c:euclidean-domain).
links.why: It gives the Euclidean algorithm and unique factorization for Gaussian integers.

steps: Take the [ring of integers adjoined](c:zsqrtd) $\sqrt d$ for an integer $d$, which has the elements $a+b\sqrt d$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Choose $d=-1$, so that $\sqrt d=i$.
Then $a+b\sqrt d=a+bi$, and the ring is exactly the Gaussian integers.
links.why: It shows that the Gaussian integers are the case $d=-1$ of a whole family of quadratic rings.

reminder: Gaussian noise is random noise whose values follow a [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution).
definition: Gaussian noise is a random signal $N(t)$ in which every finite set of samples has a joint [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution). In the usual channel model the noise is also white: its samples are [independent random variables](c:independent-random-variables) with mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2$, the noise power.
examples: The thermal noise in a resistor is well modelled by Gaussian noise.
A sequence of independent samples, each normal with mean $0$ and variance $1$, is discrete-time white Gaussian noise.
Non-example: a random signal that takes only the values $+1$ and $-1$, each with probability $1/2$, is not Gaussian noise, because its values are not normally distributed.

steps: View the noise as a family of [random variables](c:random-variable) $N(t)$ indexed by the time $t$.
Gaussian noise asks that every finite set of samples $N(t_1),\dots,N(t_k)$ is jointly normal.
This joint-normality condition is exactly the definition of a [Gaussian process](c:gaussian-process).
So Gaussian noise is a Gaussian process, usually one with mean $0$.
links.why: It shows that sums and linear filters of Gaussian noise stay Gaussian.

reminder: A generalized continued fraction is a nested fraction with a head term $h$, partial numerators $a_i$ and partial denominators $b_i$.
definition: A generalized continued fraction is a possibly infinite expression $h+\dfrac{a_0}{b_0+\dfrac{a_1}{b_1+\dfrac{a_2}{b_2+\cdots}}}$ with $h$, $a_i$ and $b_i$ in a field such as $\mathbb{R}$. The number $h$ is the head term, the $a_i$ are the partial numerators and the $b_i$ are the partial denominators. The value of an infinite expression is the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) of its finite truncations, when it exists.
examples: The golden ratio is $1+\dfrac{1}{1+\dfrac{1}{1+\cdots}}$, with $h=1$ and all $a_i=b_i=1$.
Brouncker's expansion $\dfrac4\pi=1+\dfrac{1^2}{2+\dfrac{3^2}{2+\dfrac{5^2}{2+\cdots}}}$ has $h=1$, $a_i=(2i+1)^2$ and $b_i=2$.
Non-example: the sum $1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\cdots$ is a series, not a continued fraction, because no denominator holds a further fraction.

steps: Start with a generalized continued fraction with head term $h$ and terms $a_i$ and $b_i$.
Add the condition that every partial numerator $a_i$ equals $1$.
Add the condition that $h$ is an integer and every $b_i$ is a positive integer.
The result is a simple [continued fraction](c:continued-fraction).
links.why: It shows that a simple continued fraction is a generalized one with all numerators equal to $1$.

reminder: A generalized Pareto distribution has tail probability $P(X>x)=(1+\xi x/\sigma)^{-1/\xi}$ with shape $\xi$ and scale $\sigma>0$.
definition: The generalized Pareto distribution with shape $\xi$ and scale $\sigma>0$ is the [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on $x\ge0$ with [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F(x)=1-(1+\xi x/\sigma)^{-1/\xi}$ for $\xi\ne0$ and $F(x)=1-e^{-x/\sigma}$ for $\xi=0$. For $\xi<0$ the support is the bounded interval $[0,-\sigma/\xi]$. A location parameter $\mu$ shifts the support to start at $\mu$.
examples: With $\xi=0$ it is the exponential distribution with mean $\sigma$.
With $\xi>0$ its tail decays like the power $x^{-1/\xi}$, as for a shifted Pareto distribution.
With $\xi=-1$ and $\sigma=1$ it is the uniform distribution on $[0,1]$.
Non-example: the normal distribution is not a generalized Pareto distribution, because its tail decays faster than any exponential and it lives on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

reminder: A property is generic when the points that have it contain a countable intersection of dense open sets.
definition: Let $X$ be a [Baire space](c:baire-space), for example a complete metric space. A property of points of $X$ is generic when the set of points with the property contains a countable intersection of [dense](c:dense-set) [open sets](c:open-set). Such a set is residual, and in a Baire space every residual set is dense.
examples: Being an irrational number is a generic property of real numbers, because the irrationals contain the intersection of the dense open sets $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{q_k\}$ over an enumeration $q_k$ of the rationals.
In the space of real $n\times n$ matrices, having a nonzero determinant is generic: the set is open and dense.
Non-example: being a rational number is not a generic property of $\mathbb{R}$, because the rationals are countable and a residual subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.

reminder: Two integral quadratic forms share a genus when they are equivalent over $\mathbb{R}$ and over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ for every prime $p$.
definition: The genus of an integral [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) $f$ is the set of integral forms $g$ that are equivalent to $f$ over the [real numbers](c:real-number) and over the [p-adic](c:p-adic-number) integers $\mathbb{Z}_p$ for every prime $p$. Two forms are equivalent over a ring when an invertible linear change of variables over that ring turns one into the other. Equivalence over $\mathbb{Z}$ implies equivalence over all these rings, so each class of forms lies in one genus, and a positive definite genus holds finitely many classes.
examples: The forms $x^2+xy+6y^2$ and $2x^2+xy+3y^2$ have discriminant $-23$ and lie in one genus, although they are not equivalent over $\mathbb{Z}$.
The genus of $x^2+y^2$ contains only $x^2+y^2$, because the class number of the discriminant $-4$ is $1$.

Non-example: $x^2+5y^2$ and $2x^2+2xy+3y^2$ have the same discriminant $-20$, but they are in different genera, because modulo $5$ the first form represents only squares among units and the second only non-squares.

reminder: The geodesic flow moves a tangent vector along its geodesic: at time $t$ it gives the position and the velocity of the geodesic.
definition: On a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $(M,g)$, the geodesic flow $\varphi^t$ sends a tangent vector $(x,v)\in TM$ to $(\gamma(t),\gamma'(t))$, where $\gamma$ is the [geodesic](c:geodesic) with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\gamma'(0)=v$. It is a [flow](c:flow) on the [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle), defined for all $t$ when $M$ is complete, and it keeps the length $|v|$, so it restricts to the unit tangent bundle. For a fixed base point $x$, the endpoint $\gamma(1)$ gives the [exponential map](c:exponential-map) $v\mapsto\exp_x(v)$.
examples: On the flat plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ the flow is $\varphi^t(x,v)=(x+tv,v)$, a straight line at constant speed.
On the unit sphere the flow of a unit vector runs along a great circle and returns to its start after time $2\pi$.
On a closed hyperbolic surface the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle is chaotic: it is an Anosov flow.
Non-example: the gradient flow of a function on $M$ is a flow on $M$, but its curves follow the steepest ascent and are not geodesics in general.

steps: On $TM$ the geodesic equation $\ddot x^k=-\Gamma^k_{ij}\dot x^i\dot x^j$ is a first-order equation for the pair $(x,\dot x)$.
This first-order equation defines a vector field $G$ on $TM$, the geodesic spray.
The integral curve of $G$ through $(x,v)$ is $t\mapsto(\gamma(t),\gamma'(t))$ for the geodesic $\gamma$ with that initial data.
So the geodesic flow is the [flow of the vector field](c:flow-of-a-vector-field) $G$.
links.why: It shows that geodesic flow has every property of a vector field flow, such as the group law $\varphi^{s+t}=\varphi^s\varphi^t$.

reminder: The geometric realization of a simplicial set glues one standard simplex for each simplex of the set into a topological space.
definition: For a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) $X$, the geometric realization $|X|$ is the [topological space](c:topological-space) $\left(\coprod_{n\ge0}X_n\times\Delta^n\right)/\!\sim$, where each $X_n$ is discrete and $\Delta^n$ is the standard [simplex](c:simplex). The relation $\sim$ identifies $(\theta^*x,t)$ with $(x,\theta_*t)$ for every monotone map $\theta:[m]\to[n]$, so faces and degeneracies glue the simplices together.
examples: The realization of the simplicial set $\Delta^n$ is the standard $n$-simplex.
The simplicial circle $\Delta^1/\partial\Delta^1$ has the circle $S^1$ as its realization.
The realization of the nerve of a group $G$ is a classifying space $BG$.
Non-example: the singular set $\mathrm{Sing}(X)$ of a space $X$ goes the other way, from spaces to simplicial sets, so it is not a geometric realization; it is the right adjoint of realization.

steps: Start with a small [category](c:category) $C$ and form its nerve $NC$, which is a simplicial set.
Apply the geometric realization to the simplicial set $NC$.
The space $|NC|$ is the geometric realization of the category $C$.
So the realization of categories is the case of simplicial sets that are nerves.
links.why: It shows that the classifying space of a category is the geometric realization of its nerve.

reminder: A germ at a point is a class of local sections that agree on some smaller neighborhood of that point.
definition: Let $F$ be a [sheaf](c:sheaf) on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ and let $x\in X$. A germ of $F$ at $x$ is an equivalence class of pairs $(U,s)$, with $U$ an [open set](c:open-set) that contains $x$ and $s\in F(U)$, where $(U,s)\sim(V,t)$ when $s$ and $t$ agree on some open set around $x$ inside $U\cap V$. The set of germs at $x$ is the [stalk](c:stalk) $F_x=\varinjlim_{U\ni x}F(U)$.
examples: Let $f(x)=x$ and let $g(x)=x$ for $|x|<1$ and $g(x)=0$ otherwise. The two functions have the same germ at $0$.
In the sheaf of smooth functions on $\mathbb{R}$, the function $e^{-1/x^2}$ (with value $0$ at $0$) has all derivatives $0$ at $0$, yet its germ at $0$ is not the zero germ.
Non-example: $\sin x$ and $x$ agree to first order at $0$, but their germs at $0$ differ, because the functions differ on every neighborhood of $0$.

reminder: A Gerstenhaber algebra is a graded commutative algebra with a Lie bracket of degree $-1$ that is a derivation of the product.
definition: A Gerstenhaber algebra is a graded commutative [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ with a bracket $[-,-]$ of degree $-1$. The bracket makes the shifted space $A[1]$ a [graded Lie algebra](c:graded-lie-algebra), and in each argument it is a graded [derivation](c:derivation) of the product.
examples: The polyvector fields of a manifold, with the Schouten bracket, form a Gerstenhaber algebra.
The Hochschild cohomology $HH^\bullet(A,A)$ of an associative algebra, with the cup product and the Gerstenhaber bracket, is a Gerstenhaber algebra.
Non-example: an ordinary Poisson algebra in degree $0$ with a nonzero bracket is not a Gerstenhaber algebra, because its bracket has degree $0$, not $-1$.

steps: A [Poisson n-algebra](c:poisson-n-algebra) is a graded commutative algebra with a Poisson bracket of degree $1-n$.
Take $n=2$, so the bracket has degree $1-2=-1$.
A Poisson $2$-algebra then has a bracket of degree $-1$ that acts as a derivation of the product.
This is the definition of a Gerstenhaber algebra.
links.why: It shows that a Gerstenhaber algebra is the case $n=2$ of a whole family of Poisson algebras.

steps: A [BV-algebra](c:bv-algebra) is a graded commutative algebra with an operator $\Delta$ of degree $-1$, order at most two, and $\Delta^2=0$.
Define a bracket as the failure of $\Delta$ to be a derivation of the product, up to signs.
This bracket has degree $-1$ and satisfies the Jacobi and Leibniz rules.
So every BV-algebra is a Gerstenhaber algebra, and the BV case adds the operator $\Delta$.
links.why: It shows that a BV-algebra is a Gerstenhaber algebra together with a generating operator.

reminder: A Gibbs distribution gives each configuration $x$ a probability proportional to $e^{-E(x)}$, where the energy $E$ is a sum of local terms.
definition: Let $G$ be a [graph](c:graph) and let a configuration $x$ give a value $x_v$ in a finite set to each vertex $v$. A Gibbs distribution on configurations has the form $P(x)=\frac1Z\exp\big(-\sum_CV_C(x_C)\big)$, where $C$ ranges over the [cliques](c:clique) of $G$, each $V_C$ depends only on the values $x_C$ on $C$, and $Z$ is the normalizing constant, the [partition function](c:partition-function). In physics the sum is the energy $E(x)$ and $P(x)=e^{-\beta E(x)}/Z$ at inverse temperature $\beta$.
examples: The Ising model on a graph, $P(x)\propto\exp\big(\beta\sum_{uv}x_ux_v\big)$ with spins $x_v=\pm1$, is a Gibbs distribution with potentials on the edges.
A product distribution $\prod_vp_v(x_v)$ with all $p_v>0$ is a Gibbs distribution with potentials on single vertices only.
Non-example: a distribution with $P(x)=0$ for some configuration $x$ is not a Gibbs distribution, because $e^{-E(x)}$ is always positive.

steps: Fix the clique functions $V_C$ and give each of them a parameter $\theta_C$.
The distributions $P_\theta(x)=\exp\big(-\sum_C\theta_CV_C(x_C)\big)/Z(\theta)$ have the form $\exp(\langle\theta,T(x)\rangle)/Z(\theta)$.
Here $T(x)=-(V_C(x_C))_C$ is the vector of sufficient statistics.
So the Gibbs distributions with these cliques form an [exponential family](c:exponential-family).
links.why: It shows that results on exponential families, such as moment matching, apply to Gibbs distributions.

reminder: The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ consists of all $n\times n$ matrices with the bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$.
definition: For a [field](c:field) $k$, $\mathfrak{gl}_n(k)$ is the vector space of all $n\times n$ [matrices](c:matrix) over $k$ with the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$, where $AB$ is the [matrix product](c:matrix-product). This bracket is bilinear, alternating and satisfies the Jacobi identity, so $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ is a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) of dimension $n^2$.
examples: For $n=1$ the bracket is $0$, because scalars commute, so $\mathfrak{gl}_1$ is the abelian Lie algebra $k$.
For $n=2$ the matrix units give $[E_{12},E_{21}]=E_{11}-E_{22}$.
$\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb{R})$ is the Lie algebra of the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$.
Non-example: the matrices with the ordinary product $AB$ as the bracket do not form a Lie algebra, because $[A,A]=A^2$ is not $0$ in general.

steps: For a vector space $V$, the [endomorphism Lie algebra](c:endomorphism-lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ is $\mathrm{End}(V)$ with the commutator bracket.
Take $V=k^n$ with its standard basis.
Each linear map $V\to V$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, and composition of maps is the matrix product.
So $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ becomes $\mathfrak{gl}_n(k)$ with the same commutator bracket.
links.why: It shows that $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ is the coordinate form of the Lie algebra of all linear maps of a vector space.

reminder: The Gram-Schmidt process turns a linearly independent list of vectors into an orthonormal list with the same nested spans.
definition: Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) vectors in an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space). The Gram-Schmidt process sets $u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\frac{\langle v_k,u_j\rangle}{\langle u_j,u_j\rangle}u_j$ and $e_k=u_k/\|u_k\|$. The vectors $e_1,\dots,e_n$ form an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) of the span of the $v_k$, and $\mathrm{span}(e_1,\dots,e_k)=\mathrm{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ for each $k$.
examples: With the inner product $\langle p,q\rangle=\int_{-1}^1pq\,dx$, the process applied to $1,x,x^2,\dots$ gives the Legendre polynomials, up to scaling.
Non-example: the dependent list $(1,0),(2,0)$ fails, because $u_2=0$ and cannot be divided by its norm.

reminder: The Grassmannian $Gr(r,V)$ is the space of all $r$-dimensional linear subspaces of the [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$.
definition: For a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ and a [natural number](c:natural-number) $r\le\dim V$, the Grassmannian $Gr(r,V)$ is the set of all $r$-dimensional [linear subspaces](c:linear-subspace) of $V$. For $V=\mathbb{R}^n$ it is a compact manifold of dimension $r(n-r)$, with the quotient topology from the orthonormal $r$-frames of $V$.
examples: $Gr(1,\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ is the real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^n$: its points are the lines through the origin.
$Gr(2,\mathbb{R}^4)$ is a compact manifold of dimension $2\cdot2=4$.
Non-example: the set of all planes in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that miss the origin is not $Gr(2,\mathbb{R}^3)$, because a subspace always contains $0$.

steps: Set the dimension $r$ equal to $1$ in $Gr(r,V)$.
A one-dimensional subspace of $V$ is a line through the origin.
The set of all such lines is the [projective space](c:projective-space) $\mathbb{P}(V)$.
So projective space is the case $Gr(1,V)$ of the Grassmannian.
links.why: It shows that a Grassmannian is a projective space with lines replaced by subspaces of higher dimension.

steps: A [flag variety](c:flag-variety) parametrizes chains of subspaces $V_1\subset V_2\subset\cdots\subset V_k$ of fixed dimensions.
Take a chain with exactly one subspace, of dimension $r$.
Such a chain is just an $r$-dimensional subspace of $V$.
So $Gr(r,V)$ is the flag variety with one step.
links.why: It shows that Grassmannians are the simplest flag varieties, so flag variety results apply to them.

reminder: A sequence of metric spaces $X_n$ converges to $X$ when the Gromov-Hausdorff distance from $X_n$ to $X$ tends to $0$.
definition: A sequence of compact [metric spaces](c:metric-space) $X_n$ converges to $X$ in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense when $d_{GH}(X_n,X)\to0$. Here $d_{GH}(X,Y)$ is the infimum of the [Hausdorff distance](c:hausdorff-distance) $d_H(f(X),g(Y))$ over all metric spaces $Z$ and all [isometric embeddings](c:isometric-embedding) $f:X\to Z$ and $g:Y\to Z$. For non-compact spaces with base points one asks this for every closed ball of radius $R$ around the base points, which is pointed convergence.
examples: The circles of length $1/n$ converge to a single point.
The finite grids $\tfrac1n\mathbb{Z}^2\cap[0,1]^2$ converge to the unit square $[0,1]^2$.
Non-example: the two-point spaces $\{0,n\}\subset\mathbb{R}$ do not converge in the unpointed sense, because $d_{GH}$ between $n$ and $m$ points apart is at least $|n-m|/2$.

reminder: Gromov-Witten invariants count pseudoholomorphic curves of fixed genus and class in a symplectic manifold that meet given cycles.
definition: Let $(X,\omega)$ be a closed [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) with a compatible [almost complex structure](c:almost-complex-structure), and let $\beta\in H_2(X,\mathbb{Z})$. The Gromov-Witten invariant $\langle\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_n\rangle_{g,\beta}$ is the integral $\int_{[\overline M_{g,n}(X,\beta)]^{vir}}\prod_iev_i^*\gamma_i$ over the [virtual fundamental class](c:virtual-fundamental-class) of the moduli space of [stable maps](c:stable-map) of genus $g$ with $n$ marked points. When transversality holds, it counts [pseudoholomorphic curves](c:pseudoholomorphic-curve) in the class $\beta$ through cycles dual to the $\gamma_i$.
examples: For $X=\mathbb{CP}^2$, genus $0$ and the class of a line, the invariant with two point constraints is $1$: exactly one line passes through two points.
For $X=\mathbb{CP}^2$ and degree $3$, the genus $0$ invariant with $8$ point constraints is $12$, the number of rational cubics through $8$ general points.
Non-example: the Euler characteristic $\chi(X)$ is an invariant of $X$, but it does not count curves, so it is not a Gromov-Witten invariant.

reminder: A Grothendieck fibration is a functor $p:E\to B$ in which every morphism of $B$ lifts to a Cartesian morphism with a prescribed target.
definition: A Grothendieck fibration is a [functor](c:functor) $p:E\to B$ such that for every object $e$ of $E$ and every morphism $f:b\to p(e)$ of $B$ there is a [Cartesian morphism](c:cartesian-morphism) $\tilde f:f^*e\to e$ with $p(\tilde f)=f$. Cartesian means that every morphism $g:e'\to e$ with $p(g)=f\circ h$ factors as $g=\tilde f\circ\hat g$ for exactly one $\hat g$ with $p(\hat g)=h$. Then the fibers $E_b=p^{-1}(b)$ depend pseudofunctorially on $b$.
examples: The codomain functor $\mathrm{cod}:\mathrm{Arr}(C)\to C$ from the arrow category is a fibration when $C$ has [pullbacks](c:pullback), because Cartesian lifts are pullbacks.
The functor from pairs $(X,\text{vector bundle on }X)$ to spaces is a fibration, and it lifts a map $f:Y\to X$ to the pullback bundle.
Non-example: the inclusion of the one-object category onto the object $1$ of $\{0\to1\}$ is not a fibration, because the arrow $0\to1$ has no lift that ends at that object.

steps: Start with a Grothendieck fibration $p:E\to B$ with its Cartesian lifts.
Add the dual condition that every morphism $b\to b'$ of $B$ lifts to an opCartesian morphism with a prescribed source.
A functor with both lifting properties is a [bifibration](c:bifibration).
So the bifibration case adds the opCartesian lifts, and each bifibration is also a Grothendieck fibration.
links.why: It shows that a bifibration is a fibration that is also an opfibration.

steps: Start with a [discrete fibration](c:discrete-fibration) $p:E\to B$, where each morphism $f:b\to p(e)$ has exactly one lift that ends at $e$.
Uniqueness of lifts shows that each lift is Cartesian.
So $p$ has a Cartesian lift for every morphism and every target, which makes it a Grothendieck fibration.
The discrete case adds that every lift is unique, so all fibers are discrete categories.
links.why: It shows that a discrete fibration is a Grothendieck fibration whose fibers are just sets.

reminder: The Grothendieck group of a commutative monoid is the universal abelian group that receives a monoid map from it.
definition: For a [commutative monoid](c:add-comm-monoid) $M$, the Grothendieck group $K(M)$ is the set of classes of pairs $(a,b)\in M\times M$ under the [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) $(a,b)\sim(c,d)$ when $a+d+k=b+c+k$ for some $k\in M$. The class of $(a,b)$ is the formal difference $a-b$, and these classes form an [abelian group](c:abelian-group). The map $m\mapsto m-0$ from $M$ to $K(M)$ is universal among monoid maps from $M$ to abelian groups.
examples: $K(\mathbb{N},+)=\mathbb{Z}$: the pair $(a,b)$ becomes the integer $a-b$.
For the positive integers under multiplication, $K$ is the group of positive rational numbers under multiplication.
The monoid of finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field $k$ under direct sum has $K=\mathbb{Z}$, given by the dimension.
Non-example: $(\mathbb{N},+)$ itself is not a Grothendieck group, because $1$ has no additive inverse in $\mathbb{N}$.

steps: The [group completion](c:group-completion) of a monoid $M$ is the universal group with a monoid map from $M$.
Take a monoid $M$ that is commutative, written additively.
Its group completion is abelian, because the image of $M$ is a commuting set that generates it.
This abelian group is the Grothendieck group $K(M)$, built from the formal differences $a-b$.
links.why: It shows that the Grothendieck group is the group completion in the commutative case, built from differences.

reminder: A presentation $\langle S\mid R\rangle$ describes a group as the free group on the generators $S$ divided by the relations $R$.
definition: A presentation of a [group](c:group) $G$ is a set $S$ of generators and a set $R$ of relations, which are words in the [free group](c:free-group) $F(S)$, such that $G\cong F(S)/N$ where $N$ is the [normal closure](c:is-normal-closure) of $R$. We write $G=\langle S\mid R\rangle$.
examples: $\langle a\mid a^n\rangle$ presents the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/n$.
$\langle a,b\mid aba^{-1}b^{-1}\rangle$ presents $\mathbb{Z}^2$.
$\langle r,s\mid r^n,s^2,srsr\rangle$ presents the dihedral group of order $2n$.
Non-example: the generators $a,b$ with no relations do not describe a finite group, because $\langle a,b\mid\ \rangle$ is the free group, which is infinite.

steps: Start with a presentation $\langle S\mid R\rangle$ of a group $G$.
Add the condition that the set $S$ of generators is finite.
Add the condition that the set $R$ of relations is finite.
A group with such a presentation is a [finitely presentable group](c:finitely-presentable-group).
links.why: It shows that a finitely presentable group is a presentation with finitely many generators and relations.

reminder: The group ring $R[G]$ is the ring of finite formal sums $\sum a_gg$ whose product extends the product of $G$.
definition: For a [ring](c:ring) $R$ and a [group](c:group) $G$, the group ring $R[G]$ is the free [module](c:module) over $R$ with basis $G$, so its elements are the finite sums $\sum_{g\in G}a_gg$ with $a_g\in R$. The product is $\big(\sum_ga_gg\big)\big(\sum_hb_hh\big)=\sum_{g,h}a_gb_h\,gh$, which extends the product of $G$ bilinearly.
examples: For $G=\mathbb{Z}/2=\{1,s\}$ the elements of $R[G]$ are $a+bs$ with $s^2=1$, and $\mathbb{R}[G]\cong\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$.
For $G=\mathbb{Z}$ the group ring $R[G]$ is the ring of Laurent polynomials $R[t,t^{-1}]$.
Non-example: finitely supported functions $G\to R$ with the pointwise product form a different ring, because the group ring uses the convolution product.

steps: Start with the group ring $R[G]$ of a group $G$ over a ring $R$.
Choose $R=k$ to be a [field](c:field).
Then $k[G]$ is also a $k$-vector space with basis $G$, and its product is $k$-bilinear.
This is the [group algebra](c:group-algebra) of $G$ over $k$.
links.why: It shows that a group algebra is a group ring whose coefficient ring is a field.

steps: Let $M$ be a monoid and $R$ a ring; the [monoid algebra](c:add-monoid-algebra) $R[M]$ is the free $R$-module on $M$ with the product extended from $M$.
Every group is a monoid.
Taking $M=G$ gives the same sums and the same product formula as $R[G]$.
So the group ring is the monoid algebra of a group.
links.why: It shows that group rings are monoid algebras of groups, so general facts on monoid algebras apply.

reminder: A group scheme is a scheme with a multiplication, a unit and an inverse that satisfy the group laws as morphisms.
definition: A group scheme over a base scheme $S$ is a [scheme](c:scheme) $G$ over $S$ with $S$-morphisms $m:G\times_SG\to G$, $e:S\to G$ and $i:G\to G$ that satisfy the associativity, unit and inverse laws as equalities of morphisms. Equivalently, $G$ is a [group object](c:group-object) in the category of $S$-schemes, or a scheme whose functor of points $T\mapsto G(T)$ takes values in groups.
examples: The additive group $\mathbb{G}_a=\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a group scheme, with $m^*(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x$.
The multiplicative group $\mathbb{G}_m=\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}[x,x^{-1}]$ is a group scheme, with $m^*(x)=x\otimes x$.
Every [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) over a field is a commutative group scheme.
Non-example: the affine line with the product $m(x,y)=xy$ is not a group scheme, because $0$ has no inverse; the unit group $\mathbb{G}_m$ is the group scheme.

steps: A [group object](c:group-object) in a category with finite products has multiplication, unit and inverse morphisms that satisfy the group laws.
Take the category of schemes over $S$, where the fiber product over $S$ is the product.
A group object in this category is a scheme $G$ over $S$ with morphisms $m$, $e$ and $i$ as above.
So a group scheme is a group object in the category of $S$-schemes.
links.why: It shows that a group scheme is a group object, so general facts on group objects apply.

steps: Start with a group scheme $G$ over a field $k$.
Add the condition that $G$ is affine, so $G=\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ for a $k$-algebra $A$.
The morphisms $m$, $e$ and $i$ then become algebra maps that make $A$ a Hopf algebra.
So $G$ is an [affine group scheme](c:affine-group-scheme).
links.why: It shows that affine group schemes are the group schemes that correspond to Hopf algebras.

steps: Start with a group scheme $G$ over a field $k$.
Add the condition that $G=\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ with $A$ a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra.
The order of $G$ is then the number $\dim_kA$.
Such a $G$ is a [finite group scheme](c:finite-group-scheme).
links.why: It shows that a finite group scheme is a group scheme with finite order, even if it has no points over $k$.

reminder: The Gysin map of $f:X\to Y$ is the pushforward in cohomology, defined by Poincaré duality, that raises degrees by $\dim Y-\dim X$.
definition: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map of [closed oriented manifolds](c:closed-oriented-manifold) of dimensions $m$ and $n$. The Gysin map $f_!:H^k(X)\to H^{k+n-m}(Y)$ is the composite $\mathrm{PD}_Y\circ f_*\circ\mathrm{PD}_X^{-1}$ of the inverse of Poincaré duality on $X$, the [homology](c:homology) pushforward $f_*$ and Poincaré duality on $Y$. It is also called the umkehr map or the wrong-way map in [cohomology](c:cohomology).
examples: For $p:M\to\mathrm{pt}$ the map $p_!:H^n(M)\to H^0(\mathrm{pt})=\mathbb{Z}$ is the integration over the fundamental class of $M$.
For the inclusion $i:N\to M$ of a closed oriented submanifold, $i_!(1)$ is the Poincaré dual class of $N$.
Non-example: the pullback $f^*:H^k(Y)\to H^k(X)$ keeps the degree and goes from $Y$ to $X$, so it is not the Gysin map, which shifts the degree by $\dim Y-\dim X$.

reminder: A type is an h-set when any two equalities between the same two elements are equal.
definition: In homotopy type theory, a [type](c:type) $X$ is an h-set when, for all $x,y:X$, the [identity type](c:identity-type) $x=y$ is a [mere proposition](c:mere-proposition), so any two proofs of $x=y$ are equal. In homotopy terms, $X$ is a [homotopy 0-type](c:homotopy-0-type): its homotopy type has no higher homotopy.
examples: The natural numbers form an h-set.
Every type with decidable equality is an h-set, by Hedberg's theorem.
Non-example: the circle $S^1$ is not an h-set, because its loop space is equivalent to $\mathbb{Z}$, so the identity type $\mathrm{base}=\mathrm{base}$ has many distinct elements.

steps: Every type $X$ in homotopy type theory is a [homotopy type](c:homotopy-type), a space up to homotopy.
For $x,y:X$, the identity type $x=y$ is the space of paths from $x$ to $y$.
In an h-set each such path space is a mere proposition: empty or contractible, with no higher loops.
So the h-set case adds the condition that all path spaces are propositions, which makes $X$ homotopically discrete.
links.why: It shows that an h-set is a homotopy type with no higher paths, so it behaves like an ordinary set.

steps: Start with a [mere proposition](c:mere-proposition) $P$, so any two elements of $P$ are equal.
Such a $P$ is empty or, once it has an element, contractible.
In both cases every identity type $x=y$ in $P$ is again a mere proposition.
So $P$ is an h-set, and a general h-set may have many elements.
links.why: It shows that propositions are exactly the h-sets with at most one element.

reminder: A Hadamard matrix is a square matrix with entries of absolute value $1$ and pairwise orthogonal rows, so $HH^*=nI$.
definition: An $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) $H$ over the [complex numbers](c:complex-number) is a Hadamard matrix when every entry has absolute value $1$ and $HH^*=nI$, where $H^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Then the rows are pairwise orthogonal, and so are the columns; in the classical case all entries are $\pm1$.
examples: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ is a Hadamard matrix of order $2$.
The Fourier matrix $\big(e^{2\pi ijk/n}\big)_{j,k}$ is a complex Hadamard matrix of order $n$.
The Sylvester construction $H\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}H&H\\H&-H\end{pmatrix}$ doubles the order of a Hadamard matrix.
Non-example: the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has an entry $0$ and rows that are not orthogonal, so it is not a Hadamard matrix.

steps: Let $H$ be an $n\times n$ Hadamard matrix, so $HH^*=nI$.
Scale it to $U=H/\sqrt n$.
Then $UU^*=I$, so $U$ is a [unitary matrix](c:unitary-operator).
The Hadamard case adds that all entries of $U$ have the same absolute value $1/\sqrt n$.
links.why: It shows that a Hadamard matrix is, up to a scale factor, a unitary matrix with all entries of equal size.

reminder: The Hadamard product of two matrices of the same size multiplies them entry by entry.
definition: For two $m\times n$ [matrices](c:matrix) $A$ and $B$ over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the Hadamard product $A\odot B$ is the $m\times n$ matrix with entries $(A\odot B)_{ij}=A_{ij}B_{ij}$. It is also called the Schur product or the entrywise product.
examples: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\odot\begin{pmatrix}5&6\\7&8\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5&12\\21&32\end{pmatrix}$.
If $J$ is the all-ones matrix of the same size, then $A\odot J=A$.
The Hadamard product of two positive semidefinite matrices is positive semidefinite, by the Schur product theorem.
Non-example: the ordinary matrix product $AB$ is not the Hadamard product, because it sums products along a row and a column and needs matching inner sizes.

reminder: A Hahn series is a formal sum $\sum a_gt^g$ over an ordered abelian group whose support is well-ordered.
definition: Let $\Gamma$ be a [totally ordered abelian group](c:totally-ordered-abelian-group) and $k$ a [field](c:field). A Hahn series is a function $a:\Gamma\to k$ written $\sum_{g\in\Gamma}a_gt^g$ whose support $\{g:a_g\ne0\}$ is [well-ordered](c:well-order). With the termwise sum and the [convolution](c:convolution) product $(ab)_h=\sum_{g+g'=h}a_gb_{g'}$, which is a finite sum, these series form the field $k((\Gamma))$.
examples: With $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}$ the Hahn series are the formal Laurent series $k((t))$.
With $\Gamma=\mathbb{R}$ the sum $\sum_{n\ge1}t^{1-1/n}$ is a Hahn series, because its exponents $0,\tfrac12,\tfrac23,\dots$ increase and form a well-ordered set.
Non-example: $\sum_{n\ge1}t^{-n}$ is not a Hahn series over $\mathbb{Z}$, because its exponents $-1,-2,\dots$ have no least element.

steps: Start with a [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) $\sum_{n\ge0}a_nt^n$ over $k$.
Its exponents form a set of natural numbers, which is always well-ordered.
So it is a Hahn series with $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}$, and the sum and the product agree.
Hahn series also allow other ordered groups $\Gamma$ and transfinite supports, such as exponents in $\mathbb{R}$.
links.why: It shows that Hahn series extend formal power series to real exponents and infinite well-ordered supports.

steps: Take $\Gamma=\mathbb{R}$ and a coefficient field $k$.
Add the condition that, for every bound $c$, only finitely many exponents below $c$ have nonzero coefficients.
Such a support is well-ordered, so the series is a Hahn series.
The set of these series is the [Novikov field](c:novikov-field).
links.why: It shows that the Novikov field is the subfield of Hahn series with exponents that go to infinity.

steps: A [Ribenboim power series](c:ribenboim-power-series) has exponents in a partially ordered monoid, and its support is partially well-ordered.
Take a totally ordered abelian group $\Gamma$ as the monoid of exponents.
In a total order, partially well-ordered means the same as well-ordered.
So a Hahn series over $\Gamma$ is a Ribenboim power series.
links.why: It shows that Hahn series are the totally ordered case of the more general Ribenboim series.

reminder: An $(m,k)$-handlebody of genus $g$ is the disk $D^m$ with $g$ handles of index $k$ attached.
definition: An $(m,k)$-handlebody of genus $g$ is a [manifold](c:manifold) obtained from the disk $D^m$ by attaching $g$ copies of $D^k\times D^{m-k}$, each glued along $S^{k-1}\times D^{m-k}$ to the boundary [sphere](c:sphere) of the [ball](c:ball) $D^m$. In the main case $m=3$ and $k=1$ this is the solid genus-$g$ surface, a thickened wedge of $g$ circles.
examples: The $(3,1)$-handlebody of genus $0$ is the ball $D^3$, and of genus $1$ it is the solid torus $S^1\times D^2$.
The $(3,1)$-handlebody of genus $2$ is the solid double torus, whose boundary is a surface of genus $2$.
Non-example: the exterior of a nontrivial knot in $S^3$ is a compact $3$-manifold with torus boundary, but it is not a solid torus, so it is not a handlebody.

reminder: A hard-core predicate of $f$ is an efficiently computable bit of $x$ that no efficient algorithm guesses from $f(x)$ better than chance.
definition: Let $f$ be a [one-way function](c:one-way-function). A predicate $b:\{0,1\}^*\to\{0,1\}$ is hard-core for $f$ when $b$ is computable in polynomial time and, for every probabilistic polynomial-time [algorithm](c:algorithm) $A$, the [probability](c:probability) that $A(f(x))=b(x)$ for a uniform random $x$ of length $n$ is at most $\tfrac12+\varepsilon(n)$, where $\varepsilon$ is negligible.
examples: For $f(x,r)=(g(x),r)$ built from a one-way function $g$, the inner product $b(x,r)=\langle x,r\rangle\bmod2$ is hard-core, by the Goldreich-Levin theorem.
For the RSA function, the least significant bit of $x$ is hard-core, if RSA is one-way.
Non-example: a bit that $f(x)$ reveals, such as the first bit of $x$ when $f$ copies it, is not hard-core, because $A(f(x))$ reads it and is right with probability $1$.

reminder: The $n$th harmonic number is $H_n=1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\cdots+\tfrac1n$, the sum of the first $n$ reciprocals.
definition: For a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n\ge1$, the harmonic number is $H_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1k$, a [rational number](c:rational-number), and $H_0=0$. It is the $n$th partial sum of the [harmonic series](c:harmonic-series), and $H_n=\ln n+\gamma+o(1)$, where $\gamma$ is Euler's constant.
examples: For a prime $p>3$, the numerator of $H_{p-1}$ is divisible by $p^2$, which is Wolstenholme's theorem.
Non-example: the sum $1+\tfrac14+\tfrac19+\cdots+\tfrac1{n^2}$ is not a harmonic number, because it adds squared reciprocals.

reminder: The harmonic series $\sum_{n\ge1}1/n$ diverges, although its terms tend to zero.
definition: The harmonic series is the infinite [series](c:series) $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1n=1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots$ of the reciprocals of the positive integers. Its partial sums grow without bound, because $\sum_{n=1}^{2^k}\frac1n\ge1+\frac k2$.
examples: The terms $1/n$ tend to $0$, yet the series diverges, so terms that tend to zero do not give convergence.
Grouping the terms $\frac1{2^k+1},\dots,\frac1{2^{k+1}}$ gives blocks with sum at least $\frac12$, so the partial sums pass every bound.
Non-example: the alternating series $1-\tfrac12+\tfrac13-\cdots$ converges to $\ln2$, and the series $\sum1/n^2$ converges to $\pi^2/6$, so neither is the harmonic series.

reminder: A category has reflexive coequalizers when every reflexive pair of parallel morphisms has a coequalizer.
definition: A [category](c:category) $C$ has reflexive coequalizers when every [reflexive pair](c:is-reflexive-pair) $f,g:A\rightrightarrows B$ has a [coequalizer](c:coequalizer). A pair is reflexive when $f$ and $g$ have a common section $s:B\to A$, that is $fs=gs=\mathrm{id}_B$.
examples: The categories of sets, groups and topological spaces have all coequalizers, so they have reflexive coequalizers.
Every category with all colimits, such as the category of modules over a ring, has reflexive coequalizers.

Non-example: the free category on arrows $s:B\to A$ and $f,g:A\to B$ with $fs=gs=\mathrm{id}_B$ has the reflexive pair $f,g$ but no coequalizer, because neither $\mathrm{id}_B$ nor $s$ equalizes them.

reminder: An object $S$ is a separator when parallel morphisms $f,g$ with $fh=gh$ for all $h:S\to X$ are equal.
definition: In a [category](c:category), an object $S$ is a separator (or generator) when for all [parallel morphisms](c:parallel-morphisms) $f\ne g:X\to Y$ there is a morphism $h:S\to X$ with $fh\ne gh$. Equivalently, the functor $\mathrm{Hom}(S,-)$ is [faithful](c:faithful). A family of objects is separating when the same holds with $S$ taken from the family.
examples: In the category of sets, a one-point set is a separator, because maps out of it pick elements.
In the category of abelian groups, $\mathbb{Z}$ is a separator, and in modules over a ring $R$, the module $R$ is a separator.
Non-example: in the category of sets the empty set is not a separator, because there is only one map out of it, so it cannot tell apart two different maps $\{*\}\to\{a,b\}$.

reminder: The Hausdorff distance between two subsets is the smallest $\varepsilon$ such that each set lies within $\varepsilon$ of the other.
definition: For nonempty subsets $A,B$ of a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$, the Hausdorff distance is $d_H(A,B)=\max\{\sup_{a\in A}d(a,B),\sup_{b\in B}d(b,A)\}$, where $d(a,B)=\inf_{b\in B}d(a,b)$. Equivalently, it is the infimum of all $\varepsilon>0$ such that each set lies in the $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of the other. On the nonempty compact subsets of $X$ it is a metric.
examples: For two single points $\{p\}$ and $\{q\}$, the Hausdorff distance is $d(p,q)$.
In $\mathbb{R}$ the Hausdorff distance between $[0,1]$ and $[0,3]$ is $2$.
Non-example: for $A=\{0\}$ and $B=\{0,10\}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ the one-sided value $d(0,B)=0$ is not the Hausdorff distance, because $d_H(A,B)=10$.

reminder: The heat equation $\partial_tu=\alpha\Delta u$ says that the rate of change in time is a constant multiple of the Laplacian.
definition: The heat equation is the [partial differential equation](c:partial-differential-equation) $\partial u/\partial t=\alpha\,\Delta u$ for a function $u(x,t)$ of a position $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and a time $t$, where $\alpha>0$ is the diffusivity and $\Delta$ is the [Laplace operator](c:laplace-operator) in $x$. Its fundamental solution is the [heat kernel](c:heat-kernel).
examples: The function $e^{-\alpha k^2t}\sin(kx)$ solves $u_t=\alpha u_{xx}$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
The Gaussian $(4\pi\alpha t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4\alpha t)}$ solves the heat equation for $t>0$.
Non-example: the wave equation $u_{tt}=c^2\Delta u$ is not the heat equation, because it has a second derivative in time.

reminder: A heat kernel cutoff regularizes the propagator $1/p^2$ by keeping only heat times $t\ge1/\Lambda^2$, so momenta above $\Lambda$ are suppressed.
definition: A heat kernel cutoff, also called a proper-time cutoff, regularizes a propagator by writing $\frac1{p^2}=\int_0^\infty e^{-tp^2}\,dt$ and keeping only $t\ge\Lambda^{-2}$. This replaces $1/p^2$ by $e^{-p^2/\Lambda^2}/p^2$, which suppresses momenta much larger than the scale $\Lambda$. Here $e^{-tp^2}$ is the [heat kernel](c:heat-kernel) in momentum space.
examples: With the cutoff the propagator is $e^{-p^2/\Lambda^2}/p^2$, which tends to $1/p^2$ as $\Lambda\to\infty$.
At $p^2=\Lambda^2$ the regularized propagator is smaller than $1/p^2$ by the factor $e^{-1}$.
Non-example: a sharp momentum cutoff, which sets the propagator to $0$ for $|p|>\Lambda$, is not a heat kernel cutoff, because it is not smooth.

reminder: A Heegaard splitting writes a closed orientable $3$-manifold as two handlebodies of equal genus glued along their common boundary.
definition: A Heegaard splitting of a closed orientable [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) $M$ is a decomposition $M=H_1\cup_\Sigma H_2$ into two [handlebodies](c:handlebody) $H_1$ and $H_2$ of the same genus $g$ with $H_1\cap H_2=\partial H_1=\partial H_2=\Sigma$. The common boundary $\Sigma$ is a closed [surface](c:surface) of genus $g$, called the Heegaard surface, and $g$ is the genus of the splitting.
examples: The $3$-sphere $S^3$ is the union of two solid tori glued along the torus, a splitting of genus $1$.
A lens space $L(p,q)$ has a splitting of genus $1$: two solid tori glued by a homeomorphism of the boundary torus.
Non-example: cutting $S^3$ along a torus around a nontrivial knot gives a solid torus and a knot exterior; the exterior is not a handlebody, so this is not a Heegaard splitting.

reminder: A Heegner point is a point of $X_0(N)$ that comes from an $N$-isogeny of elliptic curves with complex multiplication by $\mathcal O_K$.
definition: Let $K$ be an [imaginary quadratic field](c:imaginary-quadratic-field) with [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $\mathcal O_K$, and let $N\ge1$ be such that every prime dividing $N$ splits in $K$, which is the Heegner hypothesis. A Heegner point is a point of the [modular curve](c:modular-curve) $X_0(N)$ that represents a cyclic [isogeny](c:isogeny) $E\to E'$ of degree $N$ between [elliptic curves](c:elliptic-curve) that both have complex multiplication by $\mathcal O_K$. Such points are defined over the Hilbert class field of $K$.
examples: For $K=\mathbb{Q}(i)$ and $N=5$, the prime $5=(2+i)(2-i)$ splits, and the isogeny $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}[i]\to\mathbb{C}/(2+i)^{-1}$ gives a Heegner point on $X_0(5)$.
A modular parametrization $X_0(N)\to E$ sends Heegner points to points of $E$ over the Hilbert class field of $K$, and their trace is a point of $E(K)$.
Non-example: for $K=\mathbb{Q}(i)$ and $N=3$ the prime $3$ is inert in $K$, so the Heegner hypothesis fails and there is no Heegner point on $X_0(3)$ for this $K$.

reminder: A height function measures the arithmetic complexity of a point, so that only finitely many points have height below any bound.
definition: A height function on a set of points of a variety over a [number field](c:number-field) is a function $h$ to $\mathbb{R}$ that measures arithmetic complexity. The basic case is the Weil height on [projective space](c:projective-space): for $P=[x_0:\dots:x_n]$ with coprime integer coordinates, $H(P)=\max_i|x_i|$ and $h(P)=\log H(P)$. A height has the Northcott property when $\{P:h(P)\le B\}$ is finite for every bound $B$ over a fixed number field.
examples: For a [rational number](c:rational-number) $a/b$ in lowest terms, $H(a/b)=\max(|a|,|b|)$, so $H(3/4)=4$ and $H(5)=5$.
At most $(2B+1)^2$ rational numbers have $H\le B$, which is the Northcott property for $\mathbb{Q}$.
On an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ the canonical height $\hat h$ satisfies $\hat h(2P)=4\hat h(P)$.
Non-example: the absolute value $|x|$ on $\mathbb{Q}$ is not a height, because infinitely many rational numbers $a/b$ have $|a/b|<1$.

reminder: The Heisenberg group is the non-abelian Lie group of real $3\times3$ upper triangular matrices with ones on the diagonal.
definition: The Heisenberg group is the [Lie group](c:lie-group) of the real matrices $\begin{pmatrix}1&a&c\\0&1&b\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ under the matrix product, and its [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) is the [Heisenberg Lie algebra](c:heisenberg-lie-algebra) with $[X,Y]=Z$ and $Z$ central. For a [symplectic vector space](c:symplectic-vector-space) $(V,\omega)$ the general Heisenberg group is $V\times\mathbb{R}$ with the product $(v,s)(w,t)=(v+w,\,s+t+\tfrac12\omega(v,w))$.
examples: The matrices with $a=b=0$ form the center, which is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$.
The matrices with integer entries form the discrete Heisenberg group, a lattice in the Heisenberg group.
By the Stone-von Neumann theorem, its irreducible unitary representations with a fixed nonzero central character are all equivalent to the Schrödinger representation on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.
Non-example: the group $\mathbb{R}^3$ under addition has the same dimension but is abelian; in the Heisenberg group the matrices $I+E_{12}$ and $I+E_{23}$ do not commute.

steps: Write the commutator of two elements as $[g,h]=ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$.
Every commutator in the Heisenberg group has the form $I+cE_{13}$, which is central.
So the lower central series is $H\supset Z(H)\supset1$, and it reaches the trivial group after two steps.
Hence the Heisenberg group is a [nilpotent group](c:nilpotent-group) of class $2$, and it is not abelian.
links.why: It shows that the Heisenberg group is the standard example of a non-abelian nilpotent group.

reminder: A hemisphere of $S^n$ is the set of points with last coordinate at least $0$, and it is homeomorphic to the closed ball $D^n$.
definition: For the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:|x|=1\}$, the closed upper hemisphere is $S^n_+=\{x\in S^n:x_{n+1}\ge0\}$, and the lower one is $S^n_-$ with $x_{n+1}\le0$. Projection to the first $n$ coordinates is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) from $S^n_+$ onto the closed unit [ball](c:ball) $D^n$.
examples: For $n=1$ the hemisphere is a half circle, an arc that is homeomorphic to $[-1,1]$.
For $n=2$ the upper hemisphere is a cap that is homeomorphic to the closed disk, and its boundary is the equator.
The two hemispheres of $S^n$ cover $S^n$ and meet in the equator $S^{n-1}$.
Non-example: the sphere minus one point is not a hemisphere, because it is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ and is not compact.

reminder: The Henkin construction adds witness constants to a consistent theory and builds a model from the closed terms.
definition: Let $T$ be a [consistent theory](c:consistent-theory) in a first-order language. The Henkin construction adds, for each formula $\varphi(x)$, a new constant $c_\varphi$ and the axiom $\exists x\,\varphi(x)\to\varphi(c_\varphi)$, and repeats this until no formula lacks a witness. It extends the result to a [maximal consistent](c:maximal-consistent-formulae) set of sentences, and it takes the closed terms modulo provable equality as the universe of a [model](c:model-type) of $T$.
examples: It proves Gödel's completeness theorem: every consistent first-order theory has a model.
For a consistent theory in a countable language the construction gives a countable model, because there are only countably many closed terms.
Non-example: the ultraproduct argument also builds a model of a theory whose finite parts have models, but it uses no witness constants and no term model, so it is a different construction.

reminder: A Hermite-Einstein connection has curvature of type $(1,1)$ whose contraction with the Kähler form is a constant multiple of the identity.
definition:
Let $E$ be a [complex vector bundle](c:complex-vector-bundle) with a Hermitian metric $h$ over a [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) $(X,\omega)$. A [connection](c:connection-on-a-vector-bundle) $
abla$ on $E$ that is compatible with $h$ is Hermite-Einstein when its [curvature](c:curvature) $F_
abla$ has Dolbeault type $(1,1)$ and $\Lambda_\omega F_
abla=\lambda\,\mathrm{id}_E$ for a constant $\lambda$, where $\Lambda_\omega$ is the contraction with $\omega$.
examples: Every flat unitary connection, with $F=0$, is Hermite-Einstein with $\lambda=0$.
On a Riemann surface, a unitary connection on a line bundle is Hermite-Einstein when its curvature is a constant multiple of the area form.
The Chern connection of the tangent bundle of a Kähler-Einstein manifold is Hermite-Einstein for the Kähler metric.
Non-example: a unitary connection on a line bundle with $\Lambda_\omega F=f$ for a non-constant function $f$ is not Hermite-Einstein.

steps: Let $\nabla$ be a Hermite-Einstein connection on a Hermitian bundle over a compact Kähler manifold.
The Kähler identities turn the condition $\Lambda F=\lambda\,\mathrm{id}$ into $d_\nabla^*F=0$.
So $\nabla$ satisfies the [Yang-Mills equation](c:yang-mills-equation) and is a [Yang-Mills connection](c:yang-mills-connection).
The Hermite-Einstein case adds that $F$ has type $(1,1)$ and that $\Lambda F$ is a constant multiple of the identity.
links.why: It shows that Hermite-Einstein connections are Yang-Mills connections, so Yang-Mills theory applies to them.

reminder: The $n$th Hermite polynomial is $H_n(x)=(-1)^ne^{x^2}\dfrac{d^n}{dx^n}e^{-x^2}$, a polynomial of degree $n$.
definition: For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ the physicists' Hermite polynomial is $H_n(x)=(-1)^ne^{x^2}\dfrac{d^n}{dx^n}e^{-x^2}$, a [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree $n$ in $x$. The probabilists' version is $He_n(x)=(-1)^ne^{x^2/2}\dfrac{d^n}{dx^n}e^{-x^2/2}$, and $H_n(x)=2^{n/2}He_n(\sqrt2\,x)$. The polynomials $H_n$ are [orthogonal](c:orthogonality) for the weight $e^{-x^2}$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
examples: In the probabilists' convention $He_2(x)=x^2-1$ and $He_3(x)=x^3-3x$.
The wave functions of the quantum harmonic oscillator are $H_n(x)e^{-x^2/2}$ up to normalization.
Non-example: $x^2+1$ is not a Hermite polynomial in either convention, because $\int(x^2+1)e^{-x^2}dx\ne0$, while $H_2$ must be orthogonal to $H_0=1$.

reminder: A hexagon is the regular polygon with six equal sides and six equal interior angles of $120^\circ$.
definition: The hexagon, in its standard sense, is the convex [regular polygon](c:regular-polygon) with six sides. All sides have the same length $s$, all interior angles equal $120^\circ$, and the vertices lie on a circle of radius $s$. In a broad sense a hexagon is any [polygon](c:polygon) with six sides.
examples: A honeycomb cell is a regular hexagon.
A regular hexagon with side $s$ has area $\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}s^2$.
Six equilateral triangles of side $s$ placed around a common vertex form a regular hexagon.
Non-example: a regular pentagon has only five sides, and a six-sided polygon with unequal sides is a hexagon only in the broad sense, not the regular hexagon.

steps: A [regular polygon](c:regular-polygon) with $n$ sides has $n$ equal sides and $n$ equal interior angles.
Choose the number of sides $n$ to be $6$.
Each interior angle of a regular $n$-gon is $(n-2)\cdot180^\circ/n$, which is $120^\circ$ for $n=6$.
So the hexagon is the regular polygon with $n=6$.
links.why: It shows that every fact about regular polygons holds for the hexagon with $n=6$.

reminder: A Heyting algebra is a bounded lattice in which every pair $a,b$ has an implication $a\to b$ with $c\le(a\to b)$ iff $c\wedge a\le b$.
definition: A Heyting algebra is a [lattice](c:lattice) $(L,\le,\wedge,\vee)$ with a least element $0$ and a greatest element $1$ in which, for all $a,b$, there is an element $a\to b$ such that $c\le(a\to b)$ holds exactly when $c\wedge a\le b$. So $a\to b$ is the largest $c$ with $c\wedge a\le b$. The negation is $\neg a=(a\to0)$.
examples: The open sets of a topological space form a Heyting algebra, with $U\to V$ equal to the interior of $(X\setminus U)\cup V$.
Every [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) is a Heyting algebra with $a\to b=\neg a\vee b$.
The chain $0<\tfrac12<1$ is a Heyting algebra with $a\to b=1$ if $a\le b$ and $a\to b=b$ otherwise.
Non-example: the lattice of subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not a Heyting algebra, because $\wedge$ does not distribute over $\vee$ there, and every Heyting algebra is distributive.

steps: Start with a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) $B$, which is a distributive lattice with complements.
Define $a\to b=\neg a\vee b$.
Then $c\wedge a\le b$ holds exactly when $c\le\neg a\vee b$, by distributivity and $a\wedge\neg a=0$.
So $B$ is a Heyting algebra, and the Boolean case adds the law $a\vee\neg a=1$, the [excluded middle](c:excluded-middle).
links.why: It shows that a Boolean algebra is a Heyting algebra in which the excluded middle holds.

steps: Start with a Heyting algebra $L$.
Add the condition that every subset of $L$ has a join.
Then every subset also has a meet, namely the join of its lower bounds.
The result is a [complete Heyting algebra](c:complete-heyting-algebra), also called a frame.
links.why: It shows that a complete Heyting algebra is a Heyting algebra with all infinite joins.

steps: A [lattice](c:lattice) is a partially ordered set in which every two elements have a meet and a join.
Add a least element $0$ and a greatest element $1$.
Add, for all $a$ and $b$, an element $a\to b$ that is right adjoint to the meet with $a$.
A bounded lattice with all these implications is a Heyting algebra.
links.why: It shows that a Heyting algebra is a lattice with a bound pair and an implication operation.

reminder: A Hilbert system proves theorems from many axioms and few inference rules, usually only modus ponens.
definition: A Hilbert system is a [deductive system](c:deductive-system) with many axiom schemes and few rules, usually only [modus ponens](c:modus-ponens): from $A$ and $A\to B$ infer $B$. A proof of $B$ from assumptions $\Gamma$ is a finite list of formulas that ends in $B$, where each formula is an axiom, an assumption, or follows from earlier ones by a rule.
examples: Classical propositional logic has the axioms $A\to(B\to A)$, $(A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C))$ and $(\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B)$, with modus ponens as the only rule.
The first two axioms and modus ponens prove $A\to A$ in five steps.
Non-example: natural deduction has few axioms and many rules, namely the introduction and elimination rules, so it is not a Hilbert system.

steps: A [deductive system](c:deductive-system) fixes judgments and the rules that derive them.
Choose a single judgment form, '$A$ is true', for a formula $A$.
Take many axioms and only a few rules, such as modus ponens.
A derivation is then a finite list or tree of formulas, and the system is a Hilbert system.
links.why: It shows that a Hilbert system is a deductive system with one judgment form, many axioms and few rules.

reminder: A field $K$ is Hilbertian when every irreducible polynomial in $K(T)[X]$ stays irreducible for infinitely many values $T=t$ in $K$.
definition: A [field](c:field) $K$ is Hilbertian when, for every [irreducible polynomial](c:irreducible-polynomial) $f(T,X)$ in $K(T)[X]$ that is separable in $X$, there are infinitely many $t\in K$ for which the specialization $f(t,X)$ is defined and irreducible over $K$. Hilbert's irreducibility theorem says that every [number field](c:number-field) is Hilbertian.
examples: The field $\mathbb{Q}$ and every number field are Hilbertian, by Hilbert's irreducibility theorem.
A rational function field $k(t)$ over any field $k$ is Hilbertian.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}$ is not Hilbertian, because $X^2-(T^2+1)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}(T)$, but $t^2+1$ is a square in $\mathbb{R}$ for every real $t$.

reminder: The Hochschild homology $HH_n(A,M)$ of an algebra $A$ with bimodule coefficients $M$ is $\mathrm{Tor}_n^{A^e}(M,A)$.
definition: For an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ over a commutative ring $k$, flat over $k$, and an $A$-[bimodule](c:bimodule) $M$, the Hochschild homology $HH_n(A,M)$ is the $n$th homology of the [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $C_n=M\otimes_kA^{\otimes n}$ with the differential $b(m\otimes a_1\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n)=ma_1\otimes a_2\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(-1)^im\otimes\cdots\otimes a_ia_{i+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n+(-1)^na_nm\otimes a_1\otimes\cdots\otimes a_{n-1}$. Equivalently, $HH_n(A,M)=\mathrm{Tor}_n^{A^e}(M,A)$ for the enveloping algebra $A^e=A\otimes_kA^{op}$, with the [Tor functor](c:tor-functor).
examples: $HH_0(A,M)=M/[A,M]$, and for $M=A$ this is $A/[A,A]$.
For $A=k[x]$ one gets $HH_0=k[x]$, $HH_1=k[x]\,dx$ and $HH_n=0$ for $n\ge2$.
For a smooth commutative algebra $A$ over a field of characteristic $0$, $HH_n(A,A)$ is the module of $n$-forms $\Omega^n_{A/k}$, by the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg theorem.
Non-example: Hochschild cohomology $HH^n(A,M)=\mathrm{Ext}^n_{A^e}(A,M)$ is built from a different complex, so it is not the homology $HH_n$.

reminder: The Hodge star maps $k$-forms to $(n-k)$-forms on an oriented Riemannian $n$-manifold by $\alpha\wedge\star\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle\,\mathrm{vol}$.
definition: On an oriented [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $(M,g)$ of dimension $n$, the Hodge star is the linear map $\star:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{n-k}(M)$ on [differential forms](c:differential-form) that is defined by $\alpha\wedge\star\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$ for all $k$-forms $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Here $\langle-,-\rangle_g$ is the pointwise inner product on forms, and $\mathrm{vol}_g$ is the Riemannian [volume form](c:volume-form), which needs an [orientation](c:orientation-of-a-manifold).
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^3$ one has $\star1=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$, $\star dx=dy\wedge dz$ and $\star(dx\wedge dy)=dz$.
On $k$-forms of a Riemannian $n$-manifold, $\star\star=(-1)^{k(n-k)}$.
The codifferential is built from the star and the exterior derivative: $\delta=\pm\star d\star$.
Non-example: on a non-orientable manifold the Hodge star on forms is not globally defined, because it needs a choice of orientation.

reminder: A holomorphic $1$-form on a complex manifold is locally $\sum f_i\,dz_i$ with every $f_i$ holomorphic.
definition: A holomorphic $1$-form on a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$ is a section of the holomorphic cotangent bundle: in every holomorphic chart $(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ it is $\omega=\sum_if_i(z)\,dz_i$ with [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) $f_i$. Equivalently, it is a $(1,0)$-form $\omega$ with $\bar\partial\omega=0$.
examples: On $\mathbb{C}$ the forms $dz$ and $e^z\,dz$ are holomorphic $1$-forms.
On a compact Riemann surface of genus $g$, the holomorphic $1$-forms form a vector space of dimension $g$.
On an elliptic curve $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$, the form $dz$ is a holomorphic $1$-form that is nowhere zero.
Non-example: $\bar z\,dz$ on $\mathbb{C}$ is not holomorphic, because $\bar z$ is not a holomorphic function.

steps: A complex-valued [differential form](c:differential-form) of degree $1$ on a complex manifold is locally $\sum f_i\,dz_i+\sum g_i\,d\bar z_i$ with smooth $f_i$ and $g_i$.
Require $g_i=0$, so the form has type $(1,0)$.
Require every $f_i$ to be holomorphic.
The result is a holomorphic $1$-form, a special kind of $1$-form.
links.why: It shows that a holomorphic $1$-form is a $1$-form of type $(1,0)$ with holomorphic coefficients.
